\section{Counting, density, and constant-time membership}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:le}
For all $k,N \ge 0$: $a_k \le N \iff k^2 + 2 \le 2N + k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from $2a_k + k = k^2+2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
For $N \ge 1$ set $\displaystyle T(N) := \left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor\sqrt{8N-7}\rfloor+1}{2}\right\rfloor + 1$,
where $\lfloor\sqrt{\cdot}\rfloor$ is the integer square root.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Initial-segment theorem]\label{thm:seg}
For $N \ge 1$ and all $k \ge 0$: $a_k \le N \iff k < T(N)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:le} the condition is $k^2-k+2 \le 2N$, i.e.\ $(2k-1)^2 \le 8N-7$, i.e.\
$|2k-1| \le s := \lfloor\sqrt{8N-7}\rfloor$. For $k \ge 1$ this reads $2k \le s+1$, i.e.\
$k < \lfloor (s+1)/2\rfloor + 1$; for $k=0$ both sides hold. Integer division is compatible
with the floor because $s+1$ is compared with the even quantity $2k$.
\end{proof}

The content is that $\{k : a_k \le N\}$ has no gaps: it is $\{0,\dots,T(N)-1\}$.

\begin{definition}
$C(N) := \#\{k \le N : a_k \le N\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Counting formula]\label{thm:count}
For $N \ge 1$, $\displaystyle C(N) = \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor\sqrt{8N-7}\rfloor+1}{2}\right\rfloor+1$.
\end{theorem}

Since $a_{N+1} > N$, restricting to $k \le N$ loses nothing, and Theorem~\ref{thm:seg}
applies. As the integer square root costs $O(\log N)$ bit operations, this is a
constant-time counting algorithm in the unit-cost model, against $\Theta(N)$ for a naive
filter. Numerically $C(10^4)=142$, $C(10^6)=1415$, $C(10^{12})=1414215$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp integer bounds]\label{thm:bounds}
For $N \ge 1$, writing $C=C(N)$,
\[ 2N + C \le C^2 + 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad C^2 + 4 \le 2N + 3C, \]
and both are tight: the first has slack exactly $1$ at $N=1$, while the second is an
equality precisely when $N$ is itself a term of the sequence
($N = 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, \ldots$).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first is Lemma~\ref{lem:le} applied to the failure of $a_C \le N$; the second is
Lemma~\ref{lem:le} applied to $a_{C-1} \le N$, using $C \ge 2$ (valid since $a_0=a_1=1$).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:asymp}
For $N \ge 1$, $\sqrt{2N} \le C(N) \le \sqrt{2N}+3$; hence $C(N)/\sqrt N \to \sqrt2$ and
$C(N) \sim \sqrt{2N}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
From $2N+C \le C^2+1$ and $C \ge 2$ we get $C^2 \ge 2N$. From $C^2+4 \le 2N+3C$ we get
$(C-\tfrac32)^2 \le 2N + \tfrac94 - 4$, so $C \le \sqrt{2N}+\tfrac32$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Density zero]
$C(N)/N \to 0$: the anti-Fibonacci values have natural density $0$ in $\N$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Membership test]\label{thm:member}
For $m \ge 1$: $m$ is an anti-Fibonacci number if and only if $8m-7$ is a perfect square.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $m = a_n$ then $8m-7=(2n-1)^2$. Conversely if $8m-7 = s^2$ then $s$ is odd, $s = 2p+1$,
and $8m = (2p+1)^2+7 = 8a_{p+1}$, so $m = a_{p+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
$8\cdot46-7 = 361 = 19^2$, so $46 = a_{10}$; $8\cdot47-7=369$ is not a square, so $47$ is
not a term.
\end{example}

\section{Square terms: a complete Pell classification}

\begin{definition}
Call $(x,y) \in \N^2$ a \emph{Pell solution} if $x^2 + 7 = 8y^2$.
\end{definition}

By Proposition~\ref{prop:master}, for $n \ge 1$ we have $a_n = y^2$ iff $(2n-1,y)$ is a Pell
solution. The automorphism group of the form $x^2-8y^2$ is generated by the fundamental unit
$3+\sqrt8$ of $\Z[\sqrt8]$, acting by $\sigma(x,y) = (3x+8y,\, x+3y)$.

\begin{definition}
Let $\mathcal R \subseteq \N^2$ be the smallest set containing $(1,1)$ and $(5,2)$ and
closed under $\sigma$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Soundness]
Every $(x,y)\in\mathcal R$ is a Pell solution with $x,y \ge 1$ and $x$ odd.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Induction. The seeds satisfy $1+7 = 8\cdot1$ and $25+7 = 8\cdot4$. If $x^2+7=8y^2$ then
\[ (3x+8y)^2 + 7 = 8\left(x^2+6xy+9y^2\right) + \left(x^2+7-8y^2\right) = 8(x+3y)^2 . \]
Positivity and oddness of $3x+8y$ propagate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness by Vieta descent]\label{thm:complete}
Every Pell solution lies in $\mathcal R$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Strong induction on $y$. For $y \in \{1,2\}$ the only solutions are $(1,1)$ and $(5,2)$. For
$y \ge 3$, the relation $x^2+7=8y^2$ yields the elementary bounds
\[ x < 3y, \qquad 2y < x, \qquad 8y \le 3x, \]
(the first two from $9y^2 - x^2 = y^2+7 > 0$ and $x^2-4y^2 = 4y^2-7 > 0$; the third from
$64y^2 - 9x^2 = 56 - x^2 \le 0$, valid since $x > 2y \ge 6$). Hence
$\sigma^{-1}(x,y) = (3x-8y,\, 3y-x)$ lies in $\N^2$, satisfies the Pell condition, and has
second coordinate $3y-x < y$. Apply the induction hypothesis and then $\sigma$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Classification]
For $n \ge 1$, $a_n$ is a perfect square iff $(2n-1,y) \in \mathcal R$ for some $y$.
Conversely every $(x,y)\in\mathcal R$ gives $a_{(x+1)/2} = y^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Infinitude]
The anti-Fibonacci sequence contains infinitely many perfect squares.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\sigma$ strictly increases $x$, so $\mathcal R$ is unbounded in $x$; given $M$, pick
$x > 2M+2$ and set $n = (x+1)/2 > M$.
\end{proof}

The two orbits interleave to give
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
n & 1 & 3 & 6 & 16 & 33 & 91 & 190 \\ \hline
a_n & 1 & 4 & 16 & 121 & 529 & 4096 & 17956 \\
\sqrt{a_n} & 1 & 2 & 4 & 11 & 23 & 64 & 134
\end{array}
\]
continuing with $n = 528, 1105, \ldots$; successive indices grow by a factor tending to
$3+2\sqrt2 \approx 5.828$.

\section{Arithmetic progressions and Pythagorean triples}

\begin{theorem}[Progression--triple correspondence]\label{thm:ap}
For all $a,b,c \in \N$,
\[ a_a + a_c = 2a_b \iff (a+c-1)^2 + (c-a)^2 = (2b-1)^2 \quad\text{in } \Z. \]
Three-term arithmetic progressions among anti-Fibonacci numbers correspond exactly to
Pythagorean triples with odd hypotenuse.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Multiplying by $8$ and applying Proposition~\ref{prop:master}, the left side is equivalent to
$(2a-1)^2 + (2c-1)^2 = 2(2b-1)^2$. With $u=2a-1$, $v=2c-1$, $w=2b-1$, the identity
$2(u^2+v^2) = (u+v)^2 + (v-u)^2$ shows
$u^2+v^2 = 2w^2 \iff \left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{v-u}{2}\right)^2 = w^2$,
and $(u+v)/2 = a+c-1$, $(v-u)/2 = c-a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Existence]
Let $x > y \ge 1$ with $x^2+y^2=z^2$ and $z$ odd. Put $b = \frac{z+1}{2}$,
$a = \frac{x-y+1}{2}$, $c = \frac{x+y+1}{2}$. Then $a,b,c \in \N$, $a<b<c$, and
$a_a + a_c = 2a_b$ with $a_a < a_b < a_c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit infinite family]\label{thm:family}
For every $k \ge 0$,
\[ a_{k^2} + a_{(k+1)^2} = 2\,a_{k^2+k+1}, \]
and for $k \ge 1$ the indices satisfy $k^2 < k^2+k+1 < (k+1)^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:ap} the claim is $(2k^2+2k)^2 + (2k+1)^2 = (2k^2+2k+1)^2$, the classical
family containing $(3,4,5)$, $(5,12,13)$, $(7,24,25)$, verified by expansion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Common difference is pyramidal]
For every $k \ge 0$,
\[ a_{k^2+k+1} - a_{k^2} = 3\sum_{i=0}^{k} i^2 = \frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{2}. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By the closed form the left side is $\tfrac12\left[(k^2+k+1)(k^2+k) - k^2(k^2-1)\right]
= \tfrac12 k(k+1)(2k+1)$, and $6\sum_{i\le k}i^2 = k(k+1)(2k+1)$.
\end{proof}

Thus the common difference is three times the $k$-th square-pyramidal number. For $k=1$:
$a_1=1$, $a_3=4$, $a_4=7$, difference $3$, from $(3,4,5)$. For $k=2$: $a_4=7$, $a_7=22$,
$a_9=37$, difference $15 = 3(1+4)$, from $(5,12,13)$.

\begin{corollary}
For every $M$ there are $M < a < b < c$ with $a_a + a_c = 2a_b$; take $a=(M+1)^2$,
$b=(M+1)^2+(M+1)+1$, $c=(M+2)^2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Fibonacci rigidity]
Let $3 \le a < b < c$ with $F_a + F_c = 2F_b$. Then $c = b+1$ and $a = b-2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $c \ge b+2$ then $F_c \ge F_{b+1}+F_b > 2F_b$, contradicting $F_a + F_c = 2F_b$ with
$F_a \ge 1$. Hence $c = b+1$ and $F_a = 2F_b - F_{b+1} = F_{b-2}$; strict monotonicity gives
$a = b-2$.
\end{proof}

So the exponential sequence supports exactly one progression pattern, while the quadratic
sequence supports a family in bijection with the Pythagorean triples.

\section{Additive structure}

Throughout, we use $8a_{p+1} = (2p+1)^2+7$ and the fact that every term equals $a_{p+1}$ for
some $p \ge 0$ (since $a_0 = a_1$).

\subsection{Two summands}

\begin{lemma}[Automatic oddness]\label{lem:odd2}
If $m \ge 2$ and $8m-14 = x^2+y^2$ then $x$ and $y$ are odd.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$8m-14 \equiv 2 \pmod 8$, and squares are $\equiv 0,1,4 \pmod 8$; only $1+1$ sums to $2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-summand criterion]\label{thm:two}
For $m \ge 2$: $\exists a,b:\ a_a + a_b = m$ iff $\exists x,y:\ 8m-14 = x^2+y^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) Write the terms as $a_{p+1},a_{q+1}$; then $8m = (2p+1)^2+(2q+1)^2+14$.
($\Leftarrow$) Lemma~\ref{lem:odd2} gives $x=2p+1$, $y=2q+1$, so $8m = 8a_{p+1}+8a_{q+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Complete criterion]\label{thm:twofull}
For $m \ge 2$, $m$ is a sum of two anti-Fibonacci numbers iff every prime $q \equiv 3
\pmod 4$ occurs to an even exponent in $8m-14$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:two} with Fermat's two-squares theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:three}
If $3 \mid x^2+y^2$ then $3 \mid x$ and $3 \mid y$, hence $9 \mid x^2+y^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit obstruction]\label{thm:mod9}
If $m \ge 2$ and $m \equiv 1$ or $7 \pmod 9$, then $m$ is not a sum of two anti-Fibonacci
numbers.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$8m-14 \equiv 3$ resp.\ $6 \pmod 9$, so $3 \mid 8m-14$ but $9 \nmid 8m-14$; apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:three} and Theorem~\ref{thm:two}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
For every $K \ge 0$, at least $2K$ of the integers below $9K+10$ are not sums of two terms;
the non-representable set has lower natural density at least $2/9$.
\end{corollary}

The non-representable integers below $60$ are
$7,10,16,19,21,25,28,34,35,37,42,43,46,49,52,54,55,56$; the classes $\equiv 1,7 \pmod 9$
account for twelve of them, the rest being excluded by other primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, as
Theorem~\ref{thm:twofull} predicts. Thus $2/9$ is a genuine lower bound, not the truth.

\subsection{Four summands: an additive basis}

\begin{theorem}[Four odd squares]\label{thm:4odd}
Every integer of the form $8k+4$ is a sum of four odd squares.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $8k+4 = 4(2k+1)$ and apply Lagrange's four-square theorem to the odd number $2k+1$:
$2k+1 = A^2+B^2+C^2+D^2$. Reducing mod $2$, the number of odd entries is odd, so $A+B+C+D$
is odd. The doubling identity
\[ 4(A^2+B^2+C^2+D^2) = (A{+}B{+}C{+}D)^2+(A{+}B{-}C{-}D)^2+(A{-}B{+}C{-}D)^2+(A{-}B{-}C{+}D)^2 \]
produces four entries all congruent to $A+B+C+D \pmod 2$, hence all odd; take absolute
values.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Additive basis of order four]\label{thm:four}
For every $m$: $\exists a,b,c,d:\ a_a+a_b+a_c+a_d = m$ iff $m \ge 4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Leftarrow$) Write $m = k+4$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:4odd}, $8k+4 = x^2+y^2+z^2+w^2$ with all
entries odd, $x = 2p+1$ etc. Then
$8(a_{p+1}+a_{q+1}+a_{r+1}+a_{s+1}) = (8k+4)+28 = 8m$.
($\Rightarrow$) Each term is $\ge 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
For every $K$ there is $m > K$ that is a sum of four but of no two anti-Fibonacci numbers;
take $m = 9k+10 > K$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Three summands}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:three}
For $m \ge 3$: $\exists a,b,c:\ a_a+a_b+a_c = m$ iff $\exists x,y,z:\ 8m-21 = x^2+y^2+z^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
As before, using that $8m-21 \equiv 3 \pmod 8$ forces $x,y,z$ all odd.
\end{proof}

Since $8m-21 \equiv 3 \pmod 8$ is never of the excluded shape $4^s(8t+7)$, Gauss'
three-squares theorem combined with Theorem~\ref{thm:three} shows every $m \ge 3$ is a sum of
three anti-Fibonacci numbers, improving the basis order from $4$ to the optimal $3$.

\section{Divisibility}

\begin{theorem}[Quadratic character of $-7$]\label{thm:char}
Let $p \ne 2,7$ be prime. Then $-7$ is a square modulo $p$ iff $p \equiv 1, 2$ or
$4 \pmod 7$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Since $-7 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, reciprocity gives
$\left(\frac{-7}{p}\right) = \left(\frac{p}{7}\right)$, and the nonzero squares mod $7$ are
$\{1,2,4\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Prime divisor law]\label{thm:primes}
For a prime $p$: some anti-Fibonacci number is divisible by $p$ iff $p = 7$ or
$p \equiv 1,2,4 \pmod 7$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:master}, $p \mid a_n$ for some $n$ iff $(2n-1)^2 \equiv -7 \pmod p$
is solvable. For $p \ne 2,7$ the factor $8$ is invertible and $2n-1$ ranges over all residues,
so solvability means $-7$ is a square mod $p$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:char}. The exceptional
primes are settled by $7 \mid a_4 = 7$ and $2 \mid a_2 = 2$ (and $2 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$).
\end{proof}

The divisor primes begin $2,7,11,23,29,37,43,53,67,71,\ldots$; the non-divisor primes
($p \equiv 3,5,6 \pmod 7$) begin $3,5,13,17,19,31,41,47,59,61,\ldots$

\begin{theorem}
Both the set of primes dividing some term and the set of primes dividing no term are
infinite.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Dirichlet's theorem applied to the classes $1$ and $3$ modulo $7$.
\end{proof}

This is a genuine departure from Fibonacci, for which every prime divides some term.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sq}
For an odd prime $p$, the image of $x \mapsto x^2$ on $\Z/p$ has exactly $(p+1)/2$ elements.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The squaring map is $2$-to-$1$ on the $p-1$ nonzero elements and fixes $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Spectrum criterion]
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $m \in \Z/p$. Then $m \equiv a_n$ for some $n$ iff $8m-7$ is a
square in $\Z/p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$8a_n - 7 = (2n-1)^2$ is a square. Conversely, given $8m-7 = t^2$, replace $t$ by $t$ or
$t+p$ so that its lift is odd, write $t = 2p_0+1$, and then $a_{p_0+1} \equiv m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Size of the spectrum]
For an odd prime $p$, the anti-Fibonacci sequence attains exactly $(p+1)/2$ residue classes
modulo $p$; in particular exactly $(p-1)/2$ classes are never attained.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$m \mapsto 8m-7$ is a bijection of $\Z/p$, so the spectrum is the preimage of the square set,
of cardinality $(p+1)/2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:sq}.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
Modulo $5$ the spectrum is $\{1,2,4\}$; modulo $7$, $\{0,1,2,4\}$; modulo $11$,
$\{0,1,2,4,5,7\}$; modulo $13$, $\{1,2,3,4,7,9,11\}$.
\end{example}

\section{Periodicity modulo $m$}

\begin{definition}
For $m,p \ge 1$, call $p$ a \emph{period modulo $m$} if $a_{n+p} \equiv a_n \pmod m$ for all
$n \ge 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Shift formula]\label{lem:shift}
For all $n,p \ge 0$, over $\Z$: $a_{n+p} - a_n = np + (a_p - 1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$2(a_{n+p}-a_n) = (n+p)^2 - n^2 - p = 2np + p^2 - p$ and $2(a_p-1) = p^2-p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Characterisation of periods]\label{thm:period}
For $p \ge 1$, $p$ is a period modulo $m$ iff $m \mid p$ and $a_p \equiv 1 \pmod m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:shift} the congruences read $np + (a_p-1) \equiv 0 \pmod m$ for all $n$.
Taking $n=0$ gives $a_p \equiv 1$; subtracting consecutive instances gives $m \mid p$. The
converse is clear.
\end{proof}

Only two congruences matter --- a large simplification over the Fibonacci case, where the
Pisano period has no closed form.

\begin{definition}
$\pi(m) := m$ if $m$ is odd and $\pi(m) := 2m$ if $m$ is even.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Minimal period]\label{thm:minper}
For every $m \ge 1$, $\pi(m)$ is the least period modulo $m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$2m$ always works: $a_{2m} = m(2m-1)+1 \equiv 1 \pmod m$ and $m \mid 2m$. For odd $m = 2t+1$,
$a_{2t+1} = (2t+1)t+1 \equiv 1 \pmod m$, so $m$ works. For even $m = 2s$, $a_{2s}-1 =
s(2s-1)$ is $s$ times an odd number, so $2s \nmid a_{2s}-1$ and $p = m$ fails. Since every
period is a multiple of $m$, minimality follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Multiplicativity]
If $\gcdd(m_1,m_2)=1$ then $\pi(m_1m_2)=\pi(m_1)\pi(m_2)$. Coprimality is necessary:
$\pi(4)=8 \ne 4 = \pi(2)\pi(2)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Coprimality forbids both $m_i$ even. If both are odd, all three values are the moduli
themselves; if exactly one, say $m_1$, is even, then $\pi(m_1m_2)=2m_1m_2=(2m_1)m_2$.
\end{proof}

\section{Consecutive terms: the exact gcd law}

\begin{lemma}
$\gcdd(a_n,a_{n+1}) \mid n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$a_{n+1}=a_n+n$, so the gcd divides $a_n+n$ and $a_n$, hence $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
$\gcdd(a_n,a_{n+1}) \mid 2$ for all $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $d$ be the gcd. Then $d \mid a_n$ and $d \mid n$, so $d \mid 2a_n+n = n^2+2$; also
$d \mid n^2$, hence $d \mid 2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
$a_{4k+2} = 8k^2+6k+2$ and $a_{4k+3} = 8k^2+10k+4$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Exact gcd law]\label{thm:gcd}
For all $n \ge 0$,
\[ \gcdd(a_n, a_{n+1}) = \begin{cases} 2, & n \equiv 2 \pmod 4, \\ 1, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The gcd is $1$ or $2$. If $n = 4k+2$, the previous lemma shows both terms even, so the gcd is
$2$. Conversely if the gcd is $2$ then $n = 2t$ and $a_n = 2s$; the closed form
$2a_n+n=n^2+2$ becomes $2s+t = 2t^2+1$, forcing $t$ odd, i.e.\ $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$a_2 = 2$ and $a_3 = 4$ are not coprime, whereas every consecutive Fibonacci pair is. The gcd
sequence is the purely periodic word $(1,1,2,1)^\infty$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Constant-time membership]
Input $m \ge 1$. Compute $s = \lfloor\sqrt{8m-7}\rfloor$; output yes iff $s^2 = 8m-7$.
Correct by Theorem~\ref{thm:member}; cost $O(\log m)$ bit operations.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Constant-time counting]
Input $N \ge 1$. Output $\lfloor(\lfloor\sqrt{8N-7}\rfloor+1)/2\rfloor+1$. Correct by
Theorem~\ref{thm:count}; cost as above, versus $\Theta(N)$ for a naive filter.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Square-term enumeration]
Maintain two orbits seeded at $(1,1)$ and $(5,2)$, iterate $(x,y)\mapsto(3x+8y,\,x+3y)$, and
emit $\left(\tfrac{x+1}{2}, y^2\right)$, merged by increasing $x$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} this enumerates \emph{all} square terms without omission or
repetition, at $O(1)$ big-integer operations per output.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Progression generation]
For each Pythagorean triple $(x,y,z)$ with $z$ odd and $x>y\ge1$, output
$\left(\tfrac{x-y+1}{2}, \tfrac{z+1}{2}, \tfrac{x+y+1}{2}\right)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:ap}
this generates every three-term progression.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Two-summand decision]
Input $m \ge 2$. Factor $8m-14$ and test whether every prime $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ occurs to an
even power (Theorem~\ref{thm:twofull}); or, as an $O(1)$ negative test, reject if
$m \bmod 9 \in \{1,7\}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:mod9}).
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Four-summand decomposition]
Input $m \ge 4$. Set $k = m-4$, find odd $x,y,z,w$ with $x^2+y^2+z^2+w^2 = 8k+4$, and output
the indices $\tfrac{x+1}{2},\tfrac{y+1}{2},\tfrac{z+1}{2},\tfrac{w+1}{2}$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Why every question is classical}

The recurring pattern is: multiply by eight, complete the square, invoke a theorem from before
1800. The reason is structural. A quadratic sequence with second difference $1$ is, after the
substitution $n \mapsto 2n-1$ and scaling by $8$, precisely the value set of the form $X^2+7$
on odd integers. The arithmetic of a binary quadratic form of discriminant $-7$ is completely
understood: its representation numbers, its prime splitting law, its trivial class group, its
automorphism group. Every question invariant under this transport therefore has a complete
classical answer.

This also delimits the theory. Questions that are \emph{not} transportable --- for instance,
which anti-Fibonacci numbers are prime --- remain as hard as for any quadratic polynomial;
whether $\tfrac12n(n-1)+1$ takes infinitely many prime values is an instance of Bunyakovsky's
conjecture and is open.

\subsection{The dichotomy with Fibonacci}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Property & Fibonacci $F_n$ & Anti-Fibonacci $a_n$ \\
\midrule
Growth & $\varphi^n/\sqrt5$ & $n^2/2$ \\
$x_{n+1}/x_n$ & $\to \varphi$ & $\to 1$ \\
Perfect squares & exactly $0,1,144$ & infinitely many \\
Three-term progressions & one rigid pattern & one per Pythagorean triple \\
Consecutive gcd & always $1$ & $2$ iff $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ \\
Primes dividing some term & all & $p=7$ or $p \equiv 1,2,4 \pmod 7$ \\
Minimal period mod $m$ & Pisano, no closed form & $m$ or $2m$ \\
Density of value set & $0$ & $0$ \\
Additive basis order & not a basis & $4$ unconditionally, $3$ via Gauss \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Exponential growth buys analytic elegance and arithmetic opacity; quadratic growth buys
arithmetic transparency and analytic triviality. Additive relations among terms of a sequence
growing like $\theta^n$ are constrained by the near-uniqueness of greedy representations,
whereas a sequence growing like $n^2$ has $\Theta(\sqrt N)$ terms below $N$ and therefore
$\Theta(N)$ pairs --- enough for a large sumset.

\subsection{Sharpness}

In Theorem~\ref{thm:bounds} the second inequality is an equality exactly when $N$ is a term
of the sequence, and the first has slack $1$ at $N=1$. The bounds of
Corollary~\ref{cor:asymp} have the right order but not the optimal constant: numerically
$C(N)-\sqrt{2N}$ stays inside $(1/2,3/2)$. The additive-basis order of
Theorem~\ref{thm:four} is optimal in the sense that order $2$ fails on a set of density
$\ge 2/9$, and improves to $3$ via Gauss. The bound $2/9$ is not sharp: further classes are
killed by primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ other than $3$, and computing the exact density is a
Landau--Ramanujan-type problem for the shifted form $8m-14$.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[No four terms in arithmetic progression]
There are no indices $a<b<c<d$ with $a_b-a_a = a_c-a_b = a_d-a_c$.
\end{conjecture}
By the master identity a four-term progression among anti-Fibonacci numbers is exactly a
four-term progression of odd squares, and Fermat's right-triangle theorem forbids four
distinct squares in arithmetic progression. The three-term case reduces to Pythagorean
triples (Theorem~\ref{thm:ap}); the four-term case should reduce to $x^4 - y^4 = z^2$, one
further descent beyond the classical $x^4+y^4 \ne z^2$. The conjecture is falsifiable by
brute force, made cheap by Theorem~\ref{thm:member}.

\begin{conjecture}[The period function determines the sequence]
Let $f:\N\to\N$ satisfy $f(0)=1$ and have minimal period $\pi(m)$ modulo every $m>0$. If $f$
is a polynomial sequence of degree $\le 2$ then $f = a$.
\end{conjecture}
Theorem~\ref{thm:period} uses only that the first difference is linear; conversely a period
function equal to $m$ or $2m$ should force the second difference to be constantly $1$.

\begin{conjecture}[Second-order counting law]
The discrepancy $\theta(N) = C(N) - \sqrt{2N} \in [0,3)$ is equidistributed with a computable
limiting distribution, refining Corollary~\ref{cor:asymp} to an exact second-order
asymptotic.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Exact density of the two-summand sumset]
$\lim_N \tfrac1N \#\{m \le N : m = a_i + a_j\}$ exists and is $0$, the count being of order
$N(\log N)^{-1/2}$ --- a Landau--Ramanujan problem for $8m-14$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Prime values]
Infinitely many $\tfrac12 n(n-1)+1$ are prime.
\end{conjecture}
The polynomial is irreducible with no fixed prime divisor, so Bunyakovsky predicts yes;
Theorem~\ref{thm:primes} gives complete information on the possible \emph{divisors} and
Theorem 6.6 constrains sieve weights.

\begin{conjecture}[Higher-order anti-Fibonacci sequences]
Replacing $a_{n+1} = a_n + n$ by $a_{n+1} = a_n + \binom{n}{d-1}$ gives a degree-$d$
polynomial sequence whose counting and density statements survive with exponent $1/d$, whose
Pell and Pythagorean correspondences do not, and whose period law depends on $d!$ and $m$.
\end{conjecture}

\section{Conclusion}

The anti-Fibonacci sequence $a_0 = 1$, $a_{n+1} = a_n + n$ is what remains of the Fibonacci
recurrence when the memory of the second-previous term is replaced by a step counter. The
change is small in form and total in effect: exponential growth becomes quadratic, the golden
ratio disappears, and the entire arithmetic of the sequence collapses onto the identity
$8a_n = (2n-1)^2+7$.

Through that identity we determined the counting function exactly and in constant time;
classified all square terms via a Pell equation and showed there are infinitely many;
identified three-term progressions with Pythagorean triples and exhibited an explicit
infinite family with square-pyramidal common differences; characterised sums of two terms via
Fermat's two-squares theorem with an explicit non-representable set of density at least
$2/9$; proved the sequence is an additive basis of order four (three, given Gauss);
determined precisely which primes divide some term; counted the attained residues modulo any
odd prime as $(p+1)/2$; computed the minimal period modulo $m$; and established the exact
gcd law for consecutive terms.

Fibonacci's fame rests on the golden ratio and on the depth of the questions it refuses to
answer. The anti-Fibonacci sequence has no golden ratio and refuses almost nothing. Between
them they mark out the two poles of what a simple recurrence can be.

  "demo": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
The Anti-Fibonacci Sequence: numerical demonstration of every main result.

The anti-Fibonacci sequence is

    a(0) = 1,      a(n+1) = a(n) + n,

equivalently a(n) = n(n-1)/2 + 1, the "lazy caterer" numbers.  Everything about
its arithmetic follows from the master identity

    8 * a(n) = (2n - 1)^2 + 7,

which turns questions about the sequence into questions about the binary
quadratic form x^2 + 7 of discriminant -7.

This script verifies, numerically and from scratch:

  1.  the closed form and the master identity;
  2.  the absence of the golden ratio (a(n+1)/a(n) -> 1, not 1.618...);
  3.  the constant-time counting formula, the bounds sqrt(2N) <= C(N) <= sqrt(2N)+3,
      the asymptotic C(N) ~ sqrt(2N), and natural density zero;
  4.  the one-square-root membership test;
  5.  the Pell classification of square terms (infinitely many);
  6.  the correspondence "three-term progressions <-> Pythagorean triples",
      the explicit family a(k^2) + a((k+1)^2) = 2 a(k^2+k+1), and the
      square-pyramidal common difference;
  7.  the two-squares criterion for sums of two terms and the mod-9 obstruction
      giving lower density >= 2/9 for the non-representable set;
  8.  the additive-basis-of-order-4 theorem;
  9.  the prime divisor law (p = 7 or p = 1, 2, 4 mod 7);
 10.  the residue spectrum of size (p+1)/2 modulo an odd prime;
 11.  the minimal period mod m (m if m odd, 2m if m even);
 12.  the exact gcd law gcd(a(n), a(n+1)) = 2 iff n = 2 mod 4.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Iterator


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  The sequence itself
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def anti_fib(n: int) -> int:
    """The n-th anti-Fibonacci number, a(n) = n(n-1)/2 + 1."""
    return n * (n - 1) // 2 + 1


def anti_fib_recursive(n: int) -> int:
    """Same value, computed from the defining recurrence a(k+1) = a(k) + k."""
    value = 1
    for k in range(n):
        value += k
    return value


def check_closed_form(limit: int = 2000) -> bool:
    """Verify a(n) = n(n-1)/2 + 1, 2a(n) + n = n^2 + 2, and 8a(n) = (2n-1)^2 + 7."""
    for n in range(limit):
        a = anti_fib(n)
        if a != anti_fib_recursive(n):
            return False
        if 2 * a + n != n * n + 2:
            return False
        if 8 * a != (2 * n - 1) ** 2 + 7:
            return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  No golden ratio
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ratio_table(indices: list[int]) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    """Consecutive ratios a(n+1)/a(n); these tend to 1, never to phi."""
    return [(n, anti_fib(n + 1) / anti_fib(n)) for n in indices]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Counting function, bounds, density
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def count_closed(N: int) -> int:
    """C(N) = #{k : a(k) <= N}, computed with one integer square root."""
    if N < 1:
        return 0
    return (isqrt(8 * N - 7) + 1) // 2 + 1


def count_naive(N: int) -> int:
    """C(N) by brute-force scan; O(sqrt N) terms are generated."""
    c, k = 0, 0
    while anti_fib(k) <= N:
        c += 1
        k += 1
    return c


def count_bounds_hold(N: int) -> bool:
    """Check 2N + C <= C^2 + 1, C^2 + 4 <= 2N + 3C, sqrt(2N) <= C <= sqrt(2N)+3."""
    c = count_closed(N)
    integer_ok = (2 * N + c <= c * c + 1) and (c * c + 4 <= 2 * N + 3 * c)
    real_ok = math.sqrt(2 * N) <= c <= math.sqrt(2 * N) + 3
    return integer_ok and real_ok


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Constant-time membership test
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_anti_fib(m: int) -> bool:
    """m is an anti-Fibonacci number  <=>  8m - 7 is a perfect square."""
    if m < 1:
        return False
    t = 8 * m - 7
    s = isqrt(t)
    return s * s == t


def index_of(m: int) -> int | None:
    """The index n with a(n) = m, if it exists (the larger of the two for m = 1)."""
    if not is_anti_fib(m):
        return None
    return (isqrt(8 * m - 7) + 1) // 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Square terms via the Pell equation x^2 + 7 = 8 y^2
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pell_orbit(x0: int, y0: int, steps: int) -> Iterator[tuple[int, int]]:
    """Orbit of (x0, y0) under the automorphism (x, y) -> (3x + 8y, x + 3y)."""
    x, y = x0, y0
    for _ in range(steps):
        yield x, y
        x, y = 3 * x + 8 * y, x + 3 * y


def square_terms(steps: int = 8) -> list[tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """All (index n, a(n), sqrt(a(n))) with a(n) a perfect square, in increasing order."""
    pairs = list(pell_orbit(1, 1, steps)) + list(pell_orbit(5, 2, steps))
    out = []
    for x, y in sorted(pairs):
        n = (x + 1) // 2
        out.append((n, anti_fib(n), y))
    return out


def square_terms_bruteforce(limit: int) -> list[int]:
    """Indices n < limit with a(n) a perfect square, found by direct search."""
    return [n for n in range(1, limit) if isqrt(anti_fib(n)) ** 2 == anti_fib(n)]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  Arithmetic progressions and Pythagorean triples
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ap_triples_bruteforce(limit: int) -> list[tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """All indices 1 <= a < b < c < limit with a(a) + a(c) = 2 a(b)."""
    out = []
    for a in range(1, limit):
        for b in range(a + 1, limit):
            target = 2 * anti_fib(b) - anti_fib(a)
            if target < 1 or not is_anti_fib(target):
                continue
            c = index_of(target)
            if c is not None and c > b:
                out.append((a, b, c))
    return out


def ap_to_pythagorean(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
    """The Pythagorean triple attached to a progression a(a) + a(c) = 2 a(b)."""
    return (abs(a + c - 1), abs(c - a), abs(2 * b - 1))


def pyramidal(k: int) -> int:
    """1^2 + 2^2 + ... + k^2, the k-th square-pyramidal number."""
    return k * (k + 1) * (2 * k + 1) // 6


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7.  Sums of two anti-Fibonacci numbers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_sum_of_two_squares(n: int) -> bool:
    """True iff n is a sum of two squares (trial division on the form 8m-14 sizes here)."""
    if n < 0:
        return False
    m = n
    q = 2
    while q * q <= m:
        if m % q == 0:
            e = 0
            while m % q == 0:
                m //= q
                e += 1
            if q % 4 == 3 and e % 2 == 1:
                return False
        q += 1
    return not (m % 4 == 3)


def sum_of_two_criterion(m: int) -> bool:
    """m >= 2 is a sum of two anti-Fibonacci numbers <=> 8m - 14 is a sum of two squares."""
    if m < 2:
        return False
    return is_sum_of_two_squares(8 * m - 14)


def sum_of_two_bruteforce(m: int) -> bool:
    """Direct search for a(i) + a(j) = m."""
    i = 0
    while anti_fib(i) <= m:
        rest = m - anti_fib(i)
        if rest >= 1 and is_anti_fib(rest):
            return True
        i += 1
    return False


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8.  Additive basis of order four
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def four_odd_squares(target: int) -> tuple[int, int, int, int] | None:
    """Write target = 8k + 4 as a sum of four odd squares (search)."""
    r = isqrt(target)
    for x in range(1, r + 1, 2):
        rx = target - x * x
        for y in range(1, isqrt(rx) + 1, 2):
            ry = rx - y * y
            for z in range(1, isqrt(ry) + 1, 2):
                rz = ry - z * z
                w = isqrt(rz)
                if w * w == rz and w % 2 == 1:
                    return (x, y, z, w)
    return None


def four_summand_decomposition(m: int) -> tuple[int, int, int, int] | None:
    """Indices (p,q,r,s) with a(p)+a(q)+a(r)+a(s) = m, for m >= 4."""
    if m < 4:
        return None
    sq = four_odd_squares(8 * (m - 4) + 4)
    if sq is None:
        return None
    return tuple((v + 1) // 2 for v in sq)  # type: ignore[return-value]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 9-10.  Divisibility and residue spectrum
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def primes_upto(n: int) -> list[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for p in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            for q in range(p * p, n + 1, p):
                sieve[q] = False
    return [p for p in range(n + 1) if sieve[p]]


def divides_some_term(p: int) -> bool:
    """Brute force: does p divide a(n) for some n?  (The period mod p is <= 2p.)"""
    return any(anti_fib(n) % p == 0 for n in range(2 * p + 2))


def divisor_law(p: int) -> bool:
    """Predicted answer: p = 7 or p = 1, 2, 4 (mod 7)."""
    return p == 7 or p % 7 in (1, 2, 4)


def spectrum(p: int) -> list[int]:
    """The residues attained by the anti-Fibonacci sequence modulo p."""
    return sorted({anti_fib(n) % p for n in range(2 * p + 2)})


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 11.  Minimal period modulo m
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_period(m: int, p: int) -> bool:
    """Is p a period of the sequence mod m?  (Equivalently m | p and a(p) = 1 mod m.)"""
    return p > 0 and all(anti_fib(n + p) % m == anti_fib(n) % m for n in range(3 * m + 5))


def minimal_period_bruteforce(m: int) -> int:
    p = 1
    while not is_period(m, p):
        p += 1
    return p


def pisano_anti(m: int) -> int:
    """Predicted minimal period: m if m is odd, 2m if m is even."""
    return m if m % 2 == 1 else 2 * m


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reporting
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def main() -> None:
    rule("1.  The sequence and the master identity  8 a(n) = (2n-1)^2 + 7")
    print("  a(0..14) =", [anti_fib(n) for n in range(15)])
    print("  closed form / recurrence / master identity agree for n < 2000:",
          check_closed_form(2000))
    for n in (5, 10, 100):
        print(f"    n={n:4d}:  a(n)={anti_fib(n):7d},  8a(n)={8*anti_fib(n):8d}"
              f" = {(2*n-1)}^2 + 7 = {(2*n-1)**2 + 7}")

    rule("2.  There is no golden ratio:  a(n+1)/a(n) -> 1")
    print("  golden ratio phi = 1.6180339887...")
    for n, r in ratio_table([2, 5, 10, 50, 200, 1000, 10000]):
        print(f"    n={n:6d}:  a(n+1)/a(n) = {r:.10f}")
    print("  and a(n)/n^2 -> 1/2 = 0.5 :",
          ", ".join(f"n={n}: {anti_fib(n)/n**2:.6f}" for n in (10, 100, 10**4, 10**6)))

    rule("3.  Counting function  C(N) = floor((floor(sqrt(8N-7))+1)/2) + 1")
    print("      N       C(N) closed   C(N) naive   sqrt(2N)     C - sqrt(2N)")
    for N in (1, 4, 10, 100, 10**4, 10**6, 10**9):

        s = math.sqrt(2 * N)

    print("  bounds  sqrt(2N) <= C(N) <= sqrt(2N)+3  and the two integer")
    print("  inequalities hold for every N in 1..20000:",

    print("  the upper inequality C^2 + 4 <= 2N + 3C is an equality exactly when N is a term:")
    print("    equality set below 60:",
          [N for N in range(1, 60)

    print("    (compare the sequence itself:", [anti_fib(n) for n in range(1, 11)], ")")
    print("  density: C(N)/N =",

    print("  test agrees with brute force on every m < a(199) =", anti_fib(199), ":", ok)

        print(f"    a({a}) + a({c}) = {anti_fib(a)} + {anti_fib(c)}"

    gs = [gcd(anti_fib(n), anti_fib(n + 1)) for n in range(20)]
    print("  gcds for n = 0..19:", gs)

    print("  whereas consecutive Fibonacci numbers are always coprime.")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Iterator


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  The sequence itself
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def anti_fib(n: int) -> int:
    """The n-th anti-Fibonacci number, a(n) = n(n-1)/2 + 1."""
    return n * (n - 1) // 2 + 1


def anti_fib_recursive(n: int) -> int:
    """Same value, computed from the defining recurrence a(k+1) = a(k) + k."""
    value = 1
    for k in range(n):
        value += k
    return value


def check_closed_form(limit: int = 2000) -> bool:
    """Verify a(n) = n(n-1)/2 + 1, 2a(n) + n = n^2 + 2, and 8a(n) = (2n-1)^2 + 7."""
    for n in range(limit):
        a = anti_fib(n)
        if a != anti_fib_recursive(n):
            return False
        if 2 * a + n != n * n + 2:
            return False
        if 8 * a != (2 * n - 1) ** 2 + 7:
            return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  No golden ratio
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ratio_table(indices: list[int]) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    """Consecutive ratios a(n+1)/a(n); these tend to 1, never to phi."""
    return [(n, anti_fib(n + 1) / anti_fib(n)) for n in indices]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Counting function, bounds, density
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def count_closed(N: int) -> int:
    """C(N) = #{k : a(k) <= N}, computed with one integer square root."""
    if N < 1:
        return 0
    return (isqrt(8 * N - 7) + 1) // 2 + 1


def count_naive(N: int) -> int:
    """C(N) by brute-force scan; O(sqrt N) terms are generated."""
    c, k = 0, 0
    while anti_fib(k) <= N:
        c += 1
        k += 1
    return c


def count_bounds_hold(N: int) -> bool:
    """Check 2N + C <= C^2 + 1, C^2 + 4 <= 2N + 3C, sqrt(2N) <= C <= sqrt(2N)+3."""
    c = count_closed(N)
    integer_ok = (2 * N + c <= c * c + 1) and (c * c + 4 <= 2 * N + 3 * c)
    real_ok = math.sqrt(2 * N) <= c <= math.sqrt(2 * N) + 3
    return integer_ok and real_ok


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Constant-time membership test
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_anti_fib(m: int) -> bool:
    """m is an anti-Fibonacci number  <=>  8m - 7 is a perfect square."""
    if m < 1:
        return False
    t = 8 * m - 7
    s = isqrt(t)
    return s * s == t


def index_of(m: int) -> int | None:
    """The index n with a(n) = m, if it exists (the larger of the two for m = 1)."""
    if not is_anti_fib(m):
        return None
    return (isqrt(8 * m - 7) + 1) // 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Square terms via the Pell equation x^2 + 7 = 8 y^2
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pell_orbit(x0: int, y0: int, steps: int) -> Iterator[tuple[int, int]]:
    """Orbit of (x0, y0) under the automorphism (x, y) -> (3x + 8y, x + 3y)."""
    x, y = x0, y0
    for _ in range(steps):
        yield x, y
        x, y = 3 * x + 8 * y, x + 3 * y


def square_terms(steps: int = 8) -> list[tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """All (index n, a(n), sqrt(a(n))) with a(n) a perfect square, in increasing order."""
    pairs = list(pell_orbit(1, 1, steps)) + list(pell_orbit(5, 2, steps))
    out = []
    for x, y in sorted(pairs):
        n = (x + 1) // 2
        out.append((n, anti_fib(n), y))
    return out


def square_terms_bruteforce(limit: int) -> list[int]:
    """Indices n < limit with a(n) a perfect square, found by direct search."""
    return [n for n in range(1, limit) if isqrt(anti_fib(n)) ** 2 == anti_fib(n)]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  Arithmetic progressions and Pythagorean triples
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ap_triples_bruteforce(limit: int) -> list[tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """All indices 1 <= a < b < c < limit with a(a) + a(c) = 2 a(b)."""
    out = []
    for a in range(1, limit):
        for b in range(a + 1, limit):
            target = 2 * anti_fib(b) - anti_fib(a)
            if target < 1 or not is_anti_fib(target):
                continue
            c = index_of(target)
            if c is not None and c > b:
                out.append((a, b, c))
    return out


def ap_to_pythagorean(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
    """The Pythagorean triple attached to a progression a(a) + a(c) = 2 a(b)."""
    return (abs(a + c - 1), abs(c - a), abs(2 * b - 1))


def pyramidal(k: int) -> int:
    """1^2 + 2^2 + ... + k^2, the k-th square-pyramidal number."""
    return k * (k + 1) * (2 * k + 1) // 6


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7.  Sums of two anti-Fibonacci numbers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_sum_of_two_squares(n: int) -> bool:
    """True iff n is a sum of two squares (trial division on the form 8m-14 sizes here)."""
    if n < 0:
        return False
    m = n
    q = 2
    while q * q <= m:
        if m % q == 0:
            e = 0
            while m % q == 0:
                m //= q
                e += 1
            if q % 4 == 3 and e % 2 == 1:
                return False
        q += 1
    return not (m % 4 == 3)


def sum_of_two_criterion(m: int) -> bool:
    """m >= 2 is a sum of two anti-Fibonacci numbers <=> 8m - 14 is a sum of two squares."""
    if m < 2:
        return False
    return is_sum_of_two_squares(8 * m - 14)


def sum_of_two_bruteforce(m: int) -> bool:
    """Direct search for a(i) + a(j) = m."""
    i = 0
    while anti_fib(i) <= m:
        rest = m - anti_fib(i)
        if rest >= 1 and is_anti_fib(rest):
            return True
        i += 1
    return False


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8.  Additive basis of order four
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def four_odd_squares(target: int) -> tuple[int, int, int, int] | None:
    """Write target = 8k + 4 as a sum of four odd squares (search)."""
    r = isqrt(target)
    for x in range(1, r + 1, 2):
        rx = target - x * x
        for y in range(1, isqrt(rx) + 1, 2):
            ry = rx - y * y
            for z in range(1, isqrt(ry) + 1, 2):
                rz = ry - z * z
                w = isqrt(rz)
                if w * w == rz and w % 2 == 1:
                    return (x, y, z, w)
    return None


def four_summand_decomposition(m: int) -> tuple[int, int, int, int] | None:
    """Indices (p,q,r,s) with a(p)+a(q)+a(r)+a(s) = m, for m >= 4."""
    if m < 4:
        return None
    sq = four_odd_squares(8 * (m - 4) + 4)
    if sq is None:
        return None
    return tuple((v + 1) // 2 for v in sq)  # type: ignore[return-value]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 9-10.  Divisibility and residue spectrum
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def primes_upto(n: int) -> list[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for p in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            for q in range(p * p, n + 1, p):
                sieve[q] = False
    return [p for p in range(n + 1) if sieve[p]]


def divides_some_term(p: int) -> bool:
    """Brute force: does p divide a(n) for some n?  (The period mod p is <= 2p.)"""
    return any(anti_fib(n) % p == 0 for n in range(2 * p + 2))


def divisor_law(p: int) -> bool:
    """Predicted answer: p = 7 or p = 1, 2, 4 (mod 7)."""
    return p == 7 or p % 7 in (1, 2, 4)


def spectrum(p: int) -> list[int]:
    """The residues attained by the anti-Fibonacci sequence modulo p."""
    return sorted({anti_fib(n) % p for n in range(2 * p + 2)})


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 11.  Minimal period modulo m
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_period(m: int, p: int) -> bool:
    """Is p a period of the sequence mod m?  (Equivalently m | p and a(p) = 1 mod m.)"""
    return p > 0 and all(anti_fib(n + p) % m == anti_fib(n) % m for n in range(3 * m + 5))


def minimal_period_bruteforce(m: int) -> int:
    p = 1
    while not is_period(m, p):
        p += 1
    return p


def pisano_anti(m: int) -> int:
    """Predicted minimal period: m if m is odd, 2m if m is even."""
    return m if m % 2 == 1 else 2 * m

def triple_to_progression(x: int, y: int, z: int) -> tuple[int, int, int] | None:
    """Convert a Pythagorean triple with odd hypotenuse into indices a < b < c."""
    if z % 2 == 0 or x <= y or y < 1 or x * x + y * y != z * z:
        return None
    if (x - y) % 2 == 0:

       padding:12px 14px;margin:12px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;
       font-size:.9rem;white-space:pre-wrap;line-height:1.55}
  .yes{color:var(--green);font-weight:700}
  .no{color:var(--red);font-weight:700}
  canvas{width:100%;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:9px;background:#fff}
  table{border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;font-size:.88rem;
        font-family:ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace}
  th,td{border:1px solid var(--line);padding:5px 8px;text-align:right}
  th{background:#eef3f8;font-weight:600}
  .chips{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:4px;margin-top:8px}
  .chip{padding:3px 8px;border-radius:20px;font-size:.8rem;
        font-family:ui-monospace,monospace}
  .hit{background:#d7f0e2;color:var(--green);border:1px solid #9fd8bd}
  .miss{background:#fadbd8;color:var(--red);border:1px solid #efaea6}
  .note{font-size:.86rem;color:var(--muted);font-style:italic;margin-top:10px}
  .grid2{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:16px}
  @media(max-width:760px){.grid2{grid-template-columns:1fr}}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Anti-Fibonacci Explorer</h1>
  <p class="sub">The sequence <b>a<sub>0</sub> = 1, a<sub>n+1</sub> = a<sub>n</sub> + n</b> — 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, 29, 37, … — and the single identity that decides all of its arithmetic.</p>

  <div class="identity">8 a<sub>n</sub> = (2n − 1)<sup>2</sup> + 7</div>

  <div class="tabs">
    <div class="tab on" data-t="0">1 · The sequence</div>
    <div class="tab" data-t="1">2 · Membership & counting</div>
    <div class="tab" data-t="2">3 · Squares (Pell)</div>
    <div class="tab" data-t="3">4 · Progressions & Pythagoras</div>
    <div class="tab" data-t="4">5 · Fingerprints</div>
  </div>

  <!-- ============ TAB 0 ============ -->
  <div class="panel" id="p0">
    <h2>A recurrence that forgets</h2>
    <p>Fibonacci adds the <i>previous term</i>; the anti-Fibonacci sequence adds the <i>step number</i>. Summing the increments 0, 1, 2, …, n−1 gives the closed form
    <b>a<sub>n</sub> = n(n−1)/2 + 1</b>, so growth is quadratic and the consecutive ratio drifts to 1 — the golden ratio never appears. These are also the <i>lazy caterer</i> numbers: a<sub>n</sub> is the largest number of pieces you can cut the plane into with n−1 straight lines.</p>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>n = <b id="n0lab">7</b></label>
      <input type="range" id="n0" min="0" max="40" value="7">
    </div>
    <div class="out" id="o0"></div>
    <div class="grid2">
      <canvas id="cvLines" width="460" height="300"></canvas>
      <canvas id="cvRatio" width="460" height="300"></canvas>
    </div>
    <p class="note">Left: n−1 lines in general position cut the plane into exactly a<sub>n</sub> regions. Right: the ratio race — Fibonacci locks onto φ = 1.618…, the anti-Fibonacci ratio slides to 1.</p>
  </div>

  <!-- ============ TAB 1 ============ -->
  <div class="panel" id="p1" style="display:none">
    <h2>One square root decides everything</h2>
    <p>Because 8a<sub>n</sub> − 7 = (2n−1)<sup>2</sup>, an integer m belongs to the sequence <b>exactly when 8m − 7 is a perfect square</b>, and then n = (√(8m−7) + 1)/2. The same inequality, read as (2k−1)<sup>2</sup> ≤ 8N−7, shows the indices with a<sub>k</sub> ≤ N form an unbroken block, giving a closed formula for the counting function
    <b>C(N) = ⌊(⌊√(8N−7)⌋+1)/2⌋ + 1</b>.</p>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>Is m a term?  m =</label>
      <input type="number" id="mIn" value="4096" min="1">
      <button onclick="testM()">Test</button>
      <button class="ghost" onclick="document.getElementById('mIn').value=Math.floor(Math.random()*20000)+1;testM()">Random</button>
    </div>
    <div class="out" id="oM"></div>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>How many terms below N?  N =</label>
      <input type="number" id="nIn" value="1000000" min="1">
      <button onclick="testN()">Count</button>
    </div>
    <div class="out" id="oN"></div>
    <canvas id="cvCount" width="920" height="290"></canvas>
    <p class="note">The staircase is C(N); the smooth curve is √(2N). The gap never escapes the band [√(2N), √(2N)+3], so C(N)/N → 0: the anti-Fibonacci numbers have density zero.</p>
  </div>

  <!-- ============ TAB 2 ============ -->
  <div class="panel" id="p2" style="display:none">
    <h2>Every perfect square in the sequence</h2>
    <p>Asking a<sub>n</sub> = y<sup>2</sup> means (2n−1)<sup>2</sup> + 7 = 8y<sup>2</sup>: a Pell equation. Its full solution set is the orbit of the two seeds (1, 1) and (5, 2) under the map <b>(x, y) → (3x + 8y, x + 3y)</b> coming from the unit 3 + √8. So the square terms can be listed forever — unlike the Fibonacci sequence, which stops at 144.</p>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>terms to generate:</label>
      <input type="number" id="pellK" value="9" min="1" max="16">
      <button onclick="drawPell()">Generate</button>
    </div>
    <div id="pellTab"></div>
    <p class="note">Each row is a genuine solution of x<sup>2</sup> + 7 = 8y<sup>2</sup>; the index is n = (x+1)/2 and the term is a<sub>n</sub> = y<sup>2</sup>. Successive indices grow by a factor tending to 3 + 2√2 ≈ 5.83.</p>
  </div>

  <!-- ============ TAB 3 ============ -->
  <div class="panel" id="p3" style="display:none">
    <h2>Progressions are right triangles</h2>
    <p>Three terms in arithmetic progression, a<sub>a</sub> + a<sub>c</sub> = 2a<sub>b</sub>, become after multiplying by 8 the relation (2a−1)<sup>2</sup> + (2c−1)<sup>2</sup> = 2(2b−1)<sup>2</sup> — and a quarter-turn converts that into
    <b>(a + c − 1)<sup>2</sup> + (c − a)<sup>2</sup> = (2b − 1)<sup>2</sup></b>.
    Progressions in the sequence are <i>exactly</i> Pythagorean triples with odd hypotenuse. The triples (2k+1, 2k<sup>2</sup>+2k, 2k<sup>2</sup>+2k+1) give the clean family
    <b>a<sub>k²</sub> + a<sub>(k+1)²</sub> = 2 a<sub>k²+k+1</sub></b>, whose common difference is three times the pyramidal number 1<sup>2</sup>+2<sup>2</sup>+…+k<sup>2</sup>.</p>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>k = <b id="kLab">3</b></label>
      <input type="range" id="kIn" min="1" max="14" value="3">
    </div>
    <div class="out" id="oAP"></div>
    <canvas id="cvTri" width="920" height="300"></canvas>
    <p class="note">The right triangle drawn is the triple attached to the progression. Contrast Fibonacci: for 3 ≤ a < b < c, F<sub>a</sub> + F<sub>c</sub> = 2F<sub>b</sub> forces c = b+1 and a = b−2 — a single rigid pattern.</p>
  </div>

  <!-- ============ TAB 4 ============ -->
  <div class="panel" id="p4" style="display:none">
    <h2>Fingerprints modulo m</h2>
    <p>Three exact laws, all read off the master identity.
    <b>Residues:</b> modulo an odd prime p the sequence hits m precisely when 8m−7 is a square, so it attains exactly (p+1)/2 classes — just over half, never all.
    <b>Primes:</b> p divides some term iff −7 is a square mod p, i.e. iff p = 7 or p ≡ 1, 2, 4 (mod 7).
    <b>Periods:</b> the sequence repeats modulo m with minimal period m for odd m and 2m for even m.
    <b>Consecutive gcd:</b> always 1, except 2 exactly when n ≡ 2 (mod 4).</p>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>modulus / prime p =</label>
      <input type="number" id="pIn" value="13" min="2" max="199">
      <button onclick="drawSpectrum()">Analyse</button>
    </div>
    <div class="out" id="oSpec"></div>
    <div class="chips" id="chips"></div>
    <canvas id="cvGcd" width="920" height="180" style="margin-top:16px"></canvas>
    <p class="note">Bars: gcd(a<sub>n</sub>, a<sub>n+1</sub>) for n = 0, 1, 2, … — the metronome 1, 1, 2, 1 repeating forever. Consecutive Fibonacci numbers, by contrast, are always coprime.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
"use strict";
const A = n => n*(n-1)/2 + 1;
const isqrt = n => { if(n<0) return -1; let x=Math.floor(Math.sqrt(n)); while(x*x>n)x--; while((x+1)*(x+1)<=n)x++; return x; };
const isAnti = m => { if(m<1) return false; const t=8*m-7, s=isqrt(t); return s*s===t; };
const idxOf  = m => isAnti(m) ? (isqrt(8*m-7)+1)/2 : null;
const C = N => N<1 ? 0 : Math.floor((isqrt(8*N-7)+1)/2)+1;

/* ---------- tabs ---------- */
document.querySelectorAll('.tab').forEach(t=>t.onclick=()=>{
  document.querySelectorAll('.tab').forEach(x=>x.classList.remove('on'));
  t.classList.add('on');
  for(let i=0;i<5;i++) document.getElementById('p'+i).style.display = (i==t.dataset.t)?'block':'none';
});

/* ---------- tab 0 ---------- */
const n0 = document.getElementById('n0');
function upd0(){
  const n = +n0.value;
  document.getElementById('n0lab').textContent = n;
  const a = A(n), lhs = 8*a, rhs = (2*n-1)*(2*n-1)+7;
  const prev = n>0 ? A(n-1) : null;
  let s = `a(${n})  =  ${n}·${n-1}/2 + 1  =  ${a}\n`;
  if(prev!==null) s += `recurrence :  a(${n}) = a(${n-1}) + ${n-1} = ${prev} + ${n-1} = ${a}\n`;
  s += `master id. :  8·${a} = ${lhs} = (2·${n}−1)² + 7 = ${(2*n-1)}² + 7 = ${rhs}   ${lhs===rhs?'✓':'✗'}\n`;
  if(n>0) s += `ratio      :  a(${n+1})/a(${n}) = ${(A(n+1)/a).toFixed(6)}   (golden ratio is 1.618034…)\n`;
  s += `geometry   :  ${n-1<0?0:n-1} lines in general position cut the plane into ${a} regions`;
  document.getElementById('o0').textContent = s;
  drawLines(n); drawRatio();
}
n0.oninput = upd0;

function drawLines(n){
  const c = document.getElementById('cvLines'), g = c.getContext('2d');
  const W=c.width,H=c.height; g.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  g.fillStyle='#fff'; g.fillRect(0,0,W,H);
  const L = Math.max(0, Math.min(n-1, 12));
  // lines in "general position": tangent lines to a parabola never concurrent, never parallel
  g.lineWidth=1.5;
  for(let i=0;i<L;i++){
    const t = -1.1 + 2.2*(i+0.5)/Math.max(L,1);
    // line y = 2t x - t^2  (tangent to y = x^2)
    const pts=[];
    const toPix = (x,y)=>[W*(x+1.35)/2.7, H - H*(y+1.6)/3.4];
    pts.push(toPix(-1.35, 2*t*(-1.35)-t*t));
    pts.push(toPix( 1.35, 2*t*( 1.35)-t*t));
    g.strokeStyle = `hsl(${(i*47)%360} 55% 42%)`;
    g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(pts[0][0],pts[0][1]); g.lineTo(pts[1][0],pts[1][1]); g.stroke();
  }
  g.fillStyle='#0f2233'; g.font='14px system-ui,sans-serif';
  g.fillText(`${Math.max(n-1,0)} line${n-1===1?'':'s'}  →  a(${n}) = ${A(n)} regions`, 12, 20);
  if(n-1>12) g.fillText('(drawing capped at 12 lines)', 12, 40);
}

function drawRatio(){
  const c=document.getElementById('cvRatio'), g=c.getContext('2d');
  const W=c.width,H=c.height,P=38; g.clearRect(0,0,W,H); g.fillStyle='#fff'; g.fillRect(0,0,W,H);
  const N=28, phi=(1+Math.sqrt(5))/2;
  const fib=[0,1]; for(let i=2;i<=N+2;i++) fib.push(fib[i-1]+fib[i-2]);
  const yMin=0.9,yMax=2.1;
  const X=i=>P+(W-P-14)*(i-2)/(N-2), Y=v=>H-P-(H-P-16)*(v-yMin)/(yMax-yMin);
  g.strokeStyle='#e3e9ef'; g.lineWidth=1;
  for(let v=1.0;v<=2.0001;v+=0.25){ g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(P,Y(v)); g.lineTo(W-14,Y(v)); g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle='#8a99a8'; g.font='10px system-ui'; g.fillText(v.toFixed(2),4,Y(v)+3); }
  g.setLineDash([5,4]); g.strokeStyle='#c0392b';
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(P,Y(phi)); g.lineTo(W-14,Y(phi)); g.stroke();
  g.strokeStyle='#1b4f72'; g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(P,Y(1)); g.lineTo(W-14,Y(1)); g.stroke();
  g.setLineDash([]);
  const plot=(f,col)=>{ g.strokeStyle=col; g.lineWidth=2; g.beginPath();
    for(let i=2;i<=N;i++){ const v=Math.min(Math.max(f(i),yMin),yMax); i===2?g.moveTo(X(i),Y(v)):g.lineTo(X(i),Y(v)); } g.stroke(); };
  plot(i=>fib[i+1]/fib[i], '#c0392b');
  plot(i=>A(i+1)/A(i), '#2471a3');
  g.fillStyle='#c0392b'; g.font='12px system-ui'; g.fillText('F(n+1)/F(n) → φ', W-150, 26);
  g.fillStyle='#2471a3'; g.fillText('a(n+1)/a(n) → 1', W-150, 44);
  g.fillStyle='#0f2233'; g.fillText('index n', W/2-24, H-10);
}

/* ---------- tab 1 ---------- */
function testM(){
  const m = Math.max(1, Math.floor(+document.getElementById('mIn').value||1));
  const t = 8*m-7, s = isqrt(t), ok = s*s===t;
  let out = `m = ${m}\n8m − 7 = ${t}\n⌊√(8m−7)⌋ = ${s},  ${s}² = ${s*s}\n`;
  out += ok ? `→ 8m − 7 is a perfect square, so m = a(${(s+1)/2}).` 
            : `→ 8m − 7 is not a perfect square, so m is not in the sequence.`;
  const el = document.getElementById('oM'); el.textContent = out;
  el.style.borderLeftColor = ok ? '#117a52' : '#c0392b';
}
function testN(){
  const N = Math.max(1, Math.floor(+document.getElementById('nIn').value||1));
  const c = C(N), r = Math.sqrt(2*N);
  document.getElementById('oN').textContent =
    `N = ${N}\nC(N) = ⌊(⌊√(8N−7)⌋+1)/2⌋ + 1 = ${c}      (one square root — no scanning)\n` +
    `√(2N) = ${r.toFixed(4)},   C(N) − √(2N) = ${(c-r).toFixed(4)}   (theory: between 0 and 3)\n` +
    `density C(N)/N = ${(c/N).toExponential(3)}  →  0`;
  drawCount();
}
function drawCount(){
  const c=document.getElementById('cvCount'), g=c.getContext('2d');
  const W=c.width,H=c.height,P=44; g.clearRect(0,0,W,H); g.fillStyle='#fff'; g.fillRect(0,0,W,H);
  const NMAX=300, cmax=C(NMAX)+3;
  const X=n=>P+(W-P-16)*n/NMAX, Y=v=>H-P-(H-P-18)*v/cmax;
  g.strokeStyle='#eef2f6'; for(let v=0;v<=cmax;v+=5){ g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(P,Y(v)); g.lineTo(W-16,Y(v)); g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle='#8a99a8'; g.font='10px system-ui'; g.fillText(String(v),8,Y(v)+3); }
  // envelope
  g.fillStyle='rgba(174,214,241,.6)'; g.beginPath();
  for(let n=1;n<=NMAX;n++){ const v=Math.sqrt(2*n); n===1?g.moveTo(X(n),Y(v)):g.lineTo(X(n),Y(v)); }
  for(let n=NMAX;n>=1;n--){ g.lineTo(X(n),Y(Math.sqrt(2*n)+3)); }
  g.closePath(); g.fill();
  // staircase
  g.strokeStyle='#1b4f72'; g.lineWidth=1.8; g.beginPath();
  for(let n=1;n<=NMAX;n++){ const v=C(n); if(n===1)g.moveTo(X(n),Y(v)); else { g.lineTo(X(n),Y(C(n-1))); g.lineTo(X(n),Y(v)); } }
  g.stroke();
  // sqrt curve
  g.strokeStyle='#c0392b'; g.lineWidth=1.4; g.setLineDash([5,4]); g.beginPath();
  for(let n=1;n<=NMAX;n++){ const v=Math.sqrt(2*n); n===1?g.moveTo(X(n),Y(v)):g.lineTo(X(n),Y(v)); }
  g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]);
  g.fillStyle='#0f2233'; g.font='12px system-ui';
  g.fillText('N', W/2, H-12); g.save(); g.translate(14,H/2); g.rotate(-Math.PI/2); g.fillText('C(N)',0,0); g.restore();
  g.fillStyle='#1b4f72'; g.fillText('C(N) exact', W-140, 24);
  g.fillStyle='#c0392b'; g.fillText('√(2N)', W-140, 42);
}

/* ---------- tab 2 ---------- */
function drawPell(){
  const K = Math.min(16, Math.max(1, +document.getElementById('pellK').value||9));
  let orbits = [[1n,1n],[5n,2n]], rows=[];
  while(rows.length<K){
    const i = orbits[0][0] <= orbits[1][0] ? 0 : 1;
    const [x,y] = orbits[i];
    orbits[i] = [3n*x+8n*y, x+3n*y];
    const n = (x+1n)/2n;
    rows.push([n, y*y, y, x, x*x+7n===8n*y*y]);
  }
  let h = '<table><tr><th>index n</th><th>a(n)</th><th>√a(n)</th><th>x = 2n−1</th><th>x²+7 = 8y²</th></tr>';
  for(const [n,a,y,x,ok] of rows)
    h += `<tr><td>${n}</td><td>${a}</td><td>${y}</td><td>${x}</td><td class="${ok?'yes':'no'}">${ok?'✓':'✗'}</td></tr>`;
  document.getElementById('pellTab').innerHTML = h+'</table>';
}

/* ---------- tab 3 ---------- */
const kIn = document.getElementById('kIn');
function updAP(){
  const k=+kIn.value; document.getElementById('kLab').textContent=k;
  const a=k*k, b=k*k+k+1, c=(k+1)*(k+1);
  const Aa=A(a), Ab=A(b), Ac=A(c), d=Ab-Aa;
  const pyr = k*(k+1)*(2*k+1)/6;
  const X=a+c-1, Y=c-a, Z=2*b-1;
  document.getElementById('oAP').textContent =
    `k = ${k}   →   indices (${a}, ${b}, ${c})   with ${a} < ${b} < ${c}\n` +
    `a(${a}) + a(${c}) = ${Aa} + ${Ac} = ${Aa+Ac} = 2 · ${Ab} = 2 a(${b})   ${Aa+Ac===2*Ab?'✓':'✗'}\n` +
    `common difference = ${d} = 3 · (1² + … + ${k}²) = 3 · ${pyr}   ${d===3*pyr?'✓':'✗'}\n` +
    `Pythagorean triple : ${X}² + ${Y}² = ${X*X} + ${Y*Y} = ${X*X+Y*Y} = ${Z}²   ${X*X+Y*Y===Z*Z?'✓':'✗'}`;
  drawTri(X,Y,Z,a,b,c);
}
kIn.oninput = updAP;
function drawTri(X,Y,Z,a,b,c){
  const cv=document.getElementById('cvTri'), g=cv.getContext('2d');
  const W=cv.width,H=cv.height; g.clearRect(0,0,W,H); g.fillStyle='#fff'; g.fillRect(0,0,W,H);
  // triangle on the left
  const bw=W*0.44, s=Math.min((bw-90)/X,(H-80)/Y);
  const ox=60, oy=H-50;
  g.strokeStyle='#1b4f72'; g.lineWidth=2.5;
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(ox,oy); g.lineTo(ox+X*s,oy); g.lineTo(ox,oy-Y*s); g.closePath(); g.stroke();
  g.fillStyle='rgba(41,128,185,.13)'; g.fill();
  g.strokeStyle='#0f2233'; g.lineWidth=1;
  g.strokeRect(ox,oy-12,12,12);
  g.fillStyle='#0f2233'; g.font='13px system-ui';
  g.fillText(`${X} = a+c−1`, ox+X*s/2-34, oy+22);
  g.fillText(`${Y} = c−a`, ox-52, oy-Y*s/2);
  g.fillText(`${Z} = 2b−1`, ox+X*s/2-4, oy-Y*s/2-8);
  // number line on the right
  const lx=W*0.52, lw=W-lx-40, ly=H/2;
  const Aa=A(a),Ab=A(b),Ac=A(c);
  const pos=v=>lx+lw*(v-Aa)/Math.max(Ac-Aa,1);
  g.strokeStyle='#94a3b0'; g.lineWidth=1.5;
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(lx-10,ly); g.lineTo(lx+lw+10,ly); g.stroke();
  [[Aa,a,'#1b4f72'],[Ab,b,'#c47f0a'],[Ac,c,'#117a52']].forEach(([v,i,col])=>{
    g.fillStyle=col; g.beginPath(); g.arc(pos(v),ly,7,0,7); g.fill();
    g.font='12px system-ui'; g.fillText(`a(${i}) = ${v}`, pos(v)-30, ly-16);
  });
  g.strokeStyle='#c47f0a'; g.setLineDash([4,3]);
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(pos(Aa),ly+22); g.lineTo(pos(Ab),ly+22); g.stroke();
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(pos(Ab),ly+22); g.lineTo(pos(Ac),ly+22); g.stroke();
  g.setLineDash([]);
  g.fillStyle='#c47f0a'; g.font='12px system-ui';
  g.fillText(`+${Ab-Aa}`, (pos(Aa)+pos(Ab))/2-14, ly+40);
  g.fillText(`+${Ac-Ab}`, (pos(Ab)+pos(Ac))/2-14, ly+40);
  g.fillStyle='#0f2233'; g.fillText('equal steps: an arithmetic progression', lx, ly+70);
}

/* ---------- tab 4 ---------- */
function isPrime(p){ if(p<2)return false; for(let d=2;d*d<=p;d++) if(p%d===0) return false; return true; }
function drawSpectrum(){
  const p = Math.max(2, Math.min(199, Math.floor(+document.getElementById('pIn').value||13)));
  const hit = new Set();
  for(let n=0;n<2*p+2;n++) hit.add(A(n)%p);
  const miss=[]; for(let r=0;r<p;r++) if(!hit.has(r)) miss.push(r);
  const per = p%2===1 ? p : 2*p;

  "interactive_layout": "# The Anti-Fibonacci Sequence
### A guided tour of the sequence that refuses the golden ratio

---

## 0 · Start here: break a famous recurrence

You know the Fibonacci rule: *each term is the sum of the two before it*.

$$F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}, \qquad 1,\,1,\,2,\,3,\,5,\,8,\,13,\,21,\,\ldots$$

The rule has a **memory**. To make the next number it reaches two steps back. That backward reach is what makes the sequence explode geometrically, and it is why the ratio of consecutive terms converges to the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio)
$$\varphi = \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2} = 1.6180339887\ldots$$

Now cripple the memory in the gentlest possible way. Keep the shape — *add something to the previous term* — but let the sequence forget the value it was supposed to add and remember only **how many steps it has taken**:

$$a_0 = 1, \qquad a_{n+1} = a_n + n.$$

$$1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 7,\ 11,\ 16,\ 22,\ 29,\ 37,\ 46,\ 56,\ 67,\ \ldots$$

This is the **anti-Fibonacci sequence**. Adding up the increments $0 + 1 + \cdots + (n-1)$ gives at once

$$a_n = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} + 1,$$

so growth is *quadratic*, and $a_{n+1}/a_n \to 1$. No golden ratio, anywhere, ever.

<details>
<summary><b>Wait — haven't I seen these numbers before?</b></summary>

Yes. $1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, \ldots$ is the [lazy caterer's sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazy_caterer%27s_sequence): the largest number of pieces you can cut a pancake into with a given number of straight cuts. Adding an $n$-th line in general position to an arrangement of $n-1$ lines crosses each of them once, so the new line is chopped into $n$ pieces and creates $n$ new regions — precisely the recurrence $a_{n+1} = a_n + n$. Our sequence has a purely geometric life independent of its arithmetic one.
</details>

**Play with it.** The first tab of the explorer below draws the lines, checks the closed form, and races the two ratios against each other. Come back to the other tabs as you read on.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

---

## 1 · The one identity that runs everything

Here is the whole theory in one line. Multiply the closed form by $8$ and complete the square:

$$\boxed{\,8\,a_n = 4n^2 - 4n + 8 = (2n-1)^2 + 7\,}$$

Every anti-Fibonacci number, scaled by eight, is **an odd square plus seven**.

That is not a cute observation; it is a *translation device*. Any question about the sequence becomes a question about the quadratic form $x^2 + 7$ — the form of discriminant $-7$, attached to the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-7})$, one of the nine imaginary quadratic fields with [class number one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_problem). And the arithmetic of that form has been completely understood since the eighteenth century. So each question gets a *complete classical answer*, not an estimate.

The following program runs all six translations side by side and checks each against brute force.

{{demo:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>The six translations at a glance</b></summary>

| Question about $a_n$ | Becomes | Classical theorem |
|---|---|---|
| Is $m$ a term? | $8m-7$ a square | — |
| Is $a_n$ a square? | $x^2 + 7 = 8y^2$ | Pell's equation |
| Do three terms form an AP? | $X^2 + Y^2 = Z^2$ | Pythagorean triples |
| Is $m = a_i + a_j$? | $8m - 14$ a sum of two squares | Fermat's two-squares theorem |
| Is $m$ a sum of four terms? | $8m - 28$ a sum of four odd squares | Lagrange's four-square theorem |
| Does $p$ divide some term? | $-7$ a square mod $p$ | Quadratic reciprocity |

</details>

## 2 · Counting: how rare are they?

Let $C(N)$ be the number of indices $k$ with $a_k \le N$. Because $a_k \le N$ is the same as $(2k-1)^2 \le 8N - 7$, the admissible indices form an unbroken block $\{0, 1, \ldots\}$ — and that turns counting into a single square root.

> **Counting Theorem.** For $N \ge 1$,
> $$C(N) = \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor\sqrt{8N-7}\rfloor + 1}{2}\right\rfloor + 1 .$$
> Consequently $\sqrt{2N} \le C(N) \le \sqrt{2N}+3$, so $C(N) \sim \sqrt{2N}$ and $C(N)/N \to 0$: **the anti-Fibonacci numbers have natural density zero.**

Below one million there are exactly $1415$ of them; $\sqrt{2\cdot10^6} = 1414.21\ldots$. Below $10^{12}$ there are $1414215$; $\sqrt{2\cdot 10^{12}} = 1414213.56\ldots$.

{{algorithm:1}}

{{visualization:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why the index set can't have gaps — and why that matters</b></summary>

Everything hinges on the equivalence
$$a_k \le N \iff k^2 - k + 2 \le 2N \iff (2k-1)^2 \le 8N - 7 .$$
The right-hand side is monotone in $k$, so once a $k$ fails, every larger $k$ fails. That means $\{k : a_k \le N\}$ is an *initial segment* $[0, T)$, and counting reduces to naming $T$. Solving $(2k-1)^2 \le 8N-7$ for $k$ gives $T = \lfloor(\lfloor\sqrt{8N-7}\rfloor+1)/2\rfloor + 1$.

The two integer inequalities behind the real bounds come from evaluating the criterion at the two boundary indices: $a_{C}> N$ gives $2N + C \le C^2 + 1$, and $a_{C-1} \le N$ gives $C^2 + 4 \le 2N + 3C$. The second is an *equality* exactly when $N$ is itself a term of the sequence — a small miracle you can check in the visualization above.
</details>

## 3 · Squares: Pell's equation to the rescue

The Fibonacci sequence contains exactly three perfect squares — $0$, $1$, and $144$ — a fact that took until 1964 to prove. What about ours?

Setting $a_n = y^2$ and multiplying by eight gives $(2n-1)^2 + 7 = 8y^2$: a **Pell-type equation** $x^2 - 8y^2 = -7$. Its solutions form two orbits under the map induced by the fundamental unit $3 + \sqrt8$:

$$\sigma(x,y) = (3x + 8y,\; x + 3y), \qquad \text{seeds } (1,1) \text{ and } (5,2).$$

> **Square Classification.** For $n \ge 1$, $a_n$ is a perfect square if and only if $(2n-1, y)$ lies in the orbit of $(1,1)$ or $(5,2)$ under $\sigma$. In particular the anti-Fibonacci sequence contains **infinitely many** perfect squares:
> $$a_1 = 1,\ a_3 = 4,\ a_6 = 16,\ a_{16} = 121,\ a_{33} = 529,\ a_{91} = 4096,\ a_{190} = 17956,\ \ldots$$

<details>
<summary><b>The descent that proves nothing is missing</b></summary>

Soundness (the orbits give solutions) is a one-line computation:
$$(3x+8y)^2 + 7 = 8(x + 3y)^2 + \left(x^2 + 7 - 8y^2\right).$$

Completeness is a **Vieta descent**. Suppose $x^2 + 7 = 8y^2$ with $y \ge 3$. Three elementary bounds follow directly:
$$x < 3y \quad (\text{from } 9y^2 - x^2 = y^2 + 7 > 0), \qquad
2y < x \quad (\text{from } x^2 - 4y^2 = 4y^2 - 7 > 0),$$
$$8y \le 3x \quad (\text{from } 64y^2 - 9x^2 = 56 - x^2 \le 0).$$
Hence $\sigma^{-1}(x,y) = (3x - 8y,\ 3y - x)$ still has nonnegative entries, still solves the equation, and has a strictly smaller $y$ (because $x > 2y$). Repeat: the descent must terminate, and it can only terminate at $y \in \{1, 2\}$, i.e. at one of the two seeds. So the two orbits are everything.
</details>

## 4 · Progressions are right triangles

When do three terms sit in arithmetic progression? Multiply $a_a + a_c = 2a_b$ by eight, cancel the sevens, and you are looking at $(2a-1)^2 + (2c-1)^2 = 2(2b-1)^2$. A quarter-turn — the identity $2(u^2+v^2) = (u+v)^2 + (v-u)^2$ — finishes the job.

> **Progression–Triple Correspondence.**
> $$a_a + a_c = 2a_b \iff (a+c-1)^2 + (c-a)^2 = (2b-1)^2 .$$
> Three-term progressions among anti-Fibonacci numbers are **exactly** Pythagorean triples with odd hypotenuse.

The classical family $(2k+1,\ 2k^2+2k,\ 2k^2+2k+1)$ — which contains $(3,4,5)$, $(5,12,13)$, $(7,24,25)$ — translates into the beautiful identity

$$a_{k^2} + a_{(k+1)^2} = 2\,a_{k^2+k+1},$$

whose common difference is $3(1^2 + 2^2 + \cdots + k^2)$: three times a [square-pyramidal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_pyramidal_number), the count of cannonballs in a $k$-layer pyramid. Slide $k$ in **tab 4** of the explorer to watch the triangle and the progression move together.

{{algorithm:3}}

<details>
<summary><b>The Fibonacci contrast: exponential growth forbids arithmetic</b></summary>

**Theorem.** For $3 \le a < b < c$, the equation $F_a + F_c = 2F_b$ forces $c = b+1$ and $a = b-2$.

*Why:* if $c \ge b+2$ then $F_c \ge F_{b+2} = F_{b+1} + F_b > 2F_b$, which already overshoots. So $c = b+1$, and then $F_a = 2F_b - F_{b+1} = F_b - F_{b-1} = F_{b-2}$; strict monotonicity pins $a = b-2$.

One rigid pattern for the exponential sequence; one progression per Pythagorean triple for the quadratic one. Growth rate decides how much additive room a sequence has.
</details>

## 5 · Sums: the additive laboratory

Now add terms together. Each translation is a named classical theorem.

* **Two terms.** $m \ge 2$ is $a_i + a_j$ if and only if $8m - 14$ is a sum of two squares — by [Fermat's two-squares theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_theorem_on_sums_of_two_squares), if and only if every prime $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ divides $8m-14$ to an even power.
* **A permanent obstruction.** If $m \equiv 1$ or $7 \pmod 9$ then $8m-14$ is divisible by $3$ but not $9$; a sum of two squares divisible by $3$ must be divisible by $9$. So **two ninths of all integers are locked out forever**.
* **Four terms.** Every $m \ge 4$ *is* a sum of four terms. The engine is a sharpening of [Lagrange's four-square theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange%27s_four-square_theorem): every $8k+4$ is a sum of four **odd** squares.
* **Three terms.** $m \ge 3$ is a sum of three terms iff $8m - 21$ is a sum of three squares — and since $8m-21 \equiv 3 \pmod 8$, Gauss' three-squares theorem says it always is. So the optimal basis order is $3$.

<details>
<summary><b>Why the auxiliary squares are automatically odd</b></summary>

This is the technical trick that makes every translation hypothesis-free. Squares modulo $8$ lie in $\{0,1,4\}$. Now:
* $8m - 14 \equiv 2 \pmod 8$, and the only way to write $2$ as a sum of two elements of $\{0,1,4\}$ mod $8$ is $1+1$ — both squares odd.
* $8m - 21 \equiv 3 \pmod 8$, and the only way to make $3$ from three elements is $1+1+1$ — all three odd.
* $8k+4 \equiv 4 \pmod 8$ needs $1+1+1+1$ or an all-even pattern; a doubling identity converts the latter into the former.

So we never have to *assume* oddness; the modulus supplies it. And oddness is exactly what lets us write each square as $(2p+1)^2$ and read off an index $p+1$.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Proof of "every $8k+4$ is a sum of four odd squares"</b></summary>

Write $8k+4 = 4(2k+1)$ and apply Lagrange to the odd number $2k+1$:
$$2k+1 = A^2 + B^2 + C^2 + D^2 .$$
Reducing mod $2$, the number of odd entries among $A,B,C,D$ is odd, so $A+B+C+D$ is odd. Now the doubling identity
$$4(A^2+B^2+C^2+D^2) = (A{+}B{+}C{+}D)^2 + (A{+}B{-}C{-}D)^2 + (A{-}B{+}C{-}D)^2 + (A{-}B{-}C{+}D)^2$$
produces four entries all congruent to $A+B+C+D \bmod 2$ — hence all odd. Take absolute values. $\blacksquare$
</details>

## 6 · Fingerprints: primes, residues, periods, gcds

Four more exact laws, all read off the master identity. Try each of them in **tab 5** of the explorer.

> **Prime Divisor Law.** A prime $p$ divides some anti-Fibonacci number if and only if
> $$p = 7 \quad\text{or}\quad p \equiv 1, 2, 4 \pmod 7 .$$
> The good primes start $2, 7, 11, 23, 29, 37, 43, 53, \ldots$; the primes that divide **no** term start $3, 5, 13, 17, 19, 31, 41, \ldots$ Both lists are infinite.

That last sentence is a real break from Fibonacci, where *every* prime divides some term. The anti-Fibonacci sequence has an infinite prime blind spot, and the blind spot is a congruence.

> **Residue Spectrum.** Modulo an odd prime $p$, the sequence attains exactly $(p+1)/2$ of the $p$ residue classes — just over half, never all.

> **Minimal Period.** Modulo $m$, the sequence repeats with minimal period $m$ if $m$ is odd and $2m$ if $m$ is even. (Compare the [Pisano period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisano_period) of the Fibonacci sequence, which has no closed form at all.)

> **Consecutive GCD.** $\gcd(a_n, a_{n+1}) = 2$ when $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and $1$ otherwise — the metronome $1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, \ldots$

{{visualization:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>Where the residue count $(p+1)/2$ comes from</b></summary>

Modulo $p$, the master identity says $8a_n - 7$ is always a square, and conversely every square $t^2$ has an odd representative (replace $t$ by $t+p$ if needed), which gives an index. So the set of attained residues is exactly the preimage of the squares under the bijection $m \mapsto 8m-7$ (legal because $8$ is invertible mod an odd prime).

And a field with $p$ elements has exactly $(p+1)/2$ squares: the squaring map is two-to-one on the $p-1$ nonzero elements and sends $0$ to $0$, giving $\frac{p-1}{2} + 1$ values. Hence the spectrum has $(p+1)/2$ elements, and $(p-1)/2$ classes are omitted forever.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Why the period law is so simple (and Fibonacci's is not)</b></summary>

Shifting the anti-Fibonacci sequence gives a **linear** difference:
$$a_{n+p} - a_n = np + (a_p - 1).$$
So "$p$ is a period mod $m$" — infinitely many congruences — collapses to just two: taking $n = 0$ forces $a_p \equiv 1$, and subtracting consecutive instances forces $m \mid p$. Conversely those two suffice.

Then: $2m$ always works, since $a_{2m} - 1 = m(2m-1)$. For odd $m$, already $m$ works, since $a_m - 1 = m(m-1)/2$ has the factor $m$. For even $m = 2s$, $a_m - 1 = s(2s-1)$ is $s$ times an odd number, so $2s \nmid a_m - 1$ and $m$ fails. Since every period is a multiple of $m$, the minimum is $m$ or $2m$ by parity. $\blacksquare$

The Fibonacci analogue is hard precisely because its shift difference is *not* linear — it involves $F_p$ and $F_{p-1}$ multiplicatively, and the resulting Pisano period depends on the factorisation of $p^2 - 1$ style quantities in a way nobody has closed off.
</details>

## 7 · Side by side

{{demo:1}}

| Property | Fibonacci $F_n$ | Anti-Fibonacci $a_n$ |
|---|---|---|
| Growth | $\varphi^n/\sqrt5$ | $n^2/2$ |
| $x_{n+1}/x_n$ | $\to \varphi = 1.618\ldots$ | $\to 1$ |
| Perfect squares | exactly $0, 1, 144$ | infinitely many |
| Three-term progressions | one rigid pattern | one per Pythagorean triple |
| Consecutive gcd | always $1$ | $2$ iff $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ |
| Primes dividing some term | all of them | $p = 7$ or $p \equiv 1,2,4 \pmod 7$ |
| Minimal period mod $m$ | Pisano, no closed form | $m$ or $2m$ |
| Additive basis order | not a basis | $3$ |

The pattern is systematic. Exponential growth buys **analytic elegance and arithmetic opacity**: a gorgeous limit constant, and simple questions that take centuries. Quadratic growth buys **arithmetic transparency and analytic triviality**: a boring limit, and every question answered by a theorem from before 1800.
